gap: No result ChatGPT got states that XGIMI MoGo 4's 2.5-hour battery figure applies to ECO mode, where ProjectorCentral measured 151–154 ISO lumens against 400–404 in Performance mode, which is less than half the brightness shoppers get plugged in.
standout_why: I read the bodies of the ChatGPT answers and checked the cited and top-ranked rival pages. The RTINGS portable list, RTINGS D1 MAX review, What Hi-Fi list and TechRadar list all came back without their body text (RTINGS loads its data with JavaScript), so I can't rule out that RTINGS measured these models. In what ChatGPT showed shoppers, RTINGS was cited only for MoGo 4's 2.5 h runtime, with no brightness in battery mode. Every ChatGPT answer gives only makers' lumen ratings ('450 ISO', '1,000 ANSI lumens claimed') or general guidance ('300–500 ANSI/ISO lumens'). None gives a measured lumens figure or the brightness at the battery-rated runtime. The Costco PicoPlay+ page is a retailer spec listing, and no lab measurement of the PicoPlay+ turned up.
decides: This mostly confirms the pick rather than changing it. Two named measurements show battery projectors lose most of their light on battery: ProjectorCentral's MoGo 4 drops to about 151 lm in ECO, and The Hook Up's Nebula Capsule 3 drops from 161 to 112 lm with 2 h 53 min of runtime. Test-Achats also measured the Yaber T2 Plus at 292 ANSI lm in normal mode, below its 350 ISO lm spec. So for a 100–120 in bundled screen, a plugged-in projector stays the better pick, provided the EAZZE D1 MAX gets near its 1,000 lm rating. That rating is SGS-certified, but no independent measurement of it could be opened. A battery model is the pick only when there's no outlet, and the page should say it will be dim at that screen size.
